title: Two Choirs on the Wall: The Dedication of Jerusalem
summary: The chapter first lists the priests and Levites who returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, the line of high priests after Jeshua, and the heads of priestly and Levitical families in later generations. It then describes the dedication of the rebuilt wall: Levites and singers gather, the priests purify the people, gates, and wall, and two great thanksgiving choirs process in opposite directions along the top of the wall until they meet at the temple, where sacrifices are offered and the joy of Jerusalem is heard far away. Finally, officials are appointed over the storerooms so that priests, Levites, singers, and gatekeepers receive their portions.
story: This is the high point of the book of Nehemiah. The wall finished in chapter 6, the city repopulated in chapter 11, and the people recommitted to God's law in chapters 8 to 10 now come together in a single celebration. The lists at the start of the chapter connect the present generation to the first returnees under Zerubbabel and Jeshua nearly a century earlier, showing that the worship now offered stands in continuity with the worship restored at the return. The joy of this day makes the disappointments of chapter 13, which follow immediately, all the more striking.
historical:
The date of the dedication is not given, but it presumably followed soon after the wall's completion in about 445 BC and the settlement of the city. The lists in verses 1-26 cover a longer span. They begin with those who returned with Zerubbabel and the high priest Jeshua after Cyrus's decree of 539/538 BC, and they trace the high priestly line through Joiakim, Eliashib (Nehemiah's contemporary, 3:1), Joiada, Jonathan, and Jaddua (verses 10-11). An Aramaic letter from the Jewish community at Elephantine in Egypt, dated 407 BC, mentions Johanan as high priest in Jerusalem, which fits the Johanan of verses 22-23.

Verse 22 mentions “the reign of Darius the Persian”. Many scholars identify him as Darius II, who reigned from about 423 to 404 BC; others suggest Darius III, the last Persian king, defeated by Alexander the Great in the 330s BC. Either way, the lists extend beyond Nehemiah's own time, which suggests that they were updated from temple records by later editors.
cultural:
Dedicating a wall or building was a religious act: it marked the structure as belonging to God and set it apart for his purposes. Words from the same root describe the dedication of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:63) and of the second temple (Ezra 6:16), and later gave its name to the Jewish feast of Hanukkah, which commemorates the rededication of the temple in 164 BC. Before the procession, priests and Levites purified themselves and then the people, gates, and wall (verse 30), probably through washing and sacrifices, since only what was ritually clean could be presented to God.

Music was central to temple worship. Tradition traced the organization of Levitical singers and instruments to David (1 Chronicles 15-16; 25), and the chapter repeatedly appeals to his arrangements (verses 24, 36, 45-46). Cymbals, harps, and lyres were the standard temple instruments, and priests blew trumpets. The singers had settled in villages near Jerusalem (verses 28-29), probably because their temple duties came in rotation. The storerooms mentioned in verse 44 held the tithes and offerings on which priests, Levites, singers, and gatekeepers depended, since they did not farm land of their own.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1-26 are lists of priests and Levites across several generations, arranged by the terms of successive high priests. Verses 27-43 are narrative in Nehemiah's first-person voice, the last extended section of his memoir before chapter 13. The procession is carefully described: one choir goes to the right toward the Dung Gate with Ezra leading, the other to the left with Nehemiah following, and the two meet at the temple, a picture of the whole city encircled by praise and brought to the house of God. The words for joy and rejoicing cluster at the end of this section (verse 43), five times in one verse in Hebrew. Verses 44-47 return to a summary style, describing how the temple's support was organized.

outline.t: Priests and Levites who returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua
The line of high priests from Jeshua to Jaddua
Heads of priestly and Levitical families in later generations
Preparations: gathering the Levites and purifying people and wall
The first thanksgiving choir goes to the right
The second choir goes to the left with Nehemiah
Sacrifices and great joy at the house of God
Storerooms and portions for those who served

doctrines.note: Worship in this chapter is corporate and ordered: priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, leaders, women, and children all take part. The whole community gives thanks together, and the whole community supports those who lead its worship (verses 44-47).

The priests purify themselves before they purify the people, the gates, and the wall (verse 30). What is dedicated to God must be made clean, and those who lead others in worship must first be cleansed themselves.
The celebration's joy is traced to its source: they rejoiced “because God had given them great joy” (verse 43). Even gladness is received as a gift from God rather than produced by the occasion.

words.note: Chanukkah, dedication. The word describes the formal setting apart of the wall for God (verse 27). It is used of altars and of the temple, and it is the source of the name of the later Jewish festival Hanukkah. Dedication marks a finished work as belonging to God.

Todah, thanksgiving. It can mean a song or confession of praise, a thank offering, or, as here, a thanksgiving choir (verses 31, 38, 40). The two processions are named by the act they perform: giving thanks.

Simchah, joy. The chapter uses words for joy and rejoicing repeatedly (verses 27, 43, 44). The joy of the people is so great that “the joy of Jerusalem was heard from afar”, a public witness to the surrounding peoples who had mocked the wall's builders.

Taher, to be clean or to purify. In verse 30 the priests and Levites purify themselves and then the people, gates, and wall. Ritual purity was required for approaching God, and extending it to stones and gates shows the whole city being presented to him.

christ: The link here is thematic. The chapter's great celebration, when the holy city is dedicated and filled with praise, anticipates the joy the Bible associates with God's final dwelling among his people. The psalms of ascent sung by pilgrims to Jerusalem already looked for the city's peace (Psalm 122), and the New Testament points to a greater fulfillment: Jesus spoke of his own body as the temple (John 2:19-21), and the final vision of Revelation shows a holy city whose temple is the Lord God and the Lamb (Revelation 21:22). The line of high priests traced in verses 10-11 also belongs to the priesthood that Hebrews contrasts with Christ, a high priest who continues forever and does not need to be replaced by successors (Hebrews 7:23-25).

hard.q: If the list runs to Jaddua and a later Darius, how can Nehemiah have written it?
hard.a: Verses 10-11 and 22 extend the priestly lists beyond Nehemiah's own lifetime, possibly into the late fifth or even the fourth century BC. Most scholars take this as evidence that the books of Ezra and Nehemiah were compiled from several sources, including Nehemiah's personal memoir, official lists, and temple records, by an editor or editors working after Nehemiah's death. This view does not question the authenticity of Nehemiah's first-person account, which clearly comes from him, but recognizes that the book as we have it received its final form later. Jewish tradition treated Ezra and Nehemiah as one book, and some older interpreters attributed its final compilation to Ezra, which would limit how late the list could run. Others, who identify the Darius of verse 22 with Darius II, see the lists as updated only a generation after Nehemiah. The Bible itself does not claim that Nehemiah wrote every line of the book that bears his name, and ancient records were commonly brought up to date by later scribes.

questions: The two choirs walked the whole wall giving thanks before meeting at the temple. How do you mark the completion of something God has helped you do?
The priests purified themselves before purifying anyone else. What does this suggest about those who lead others in worship or service?
“The joy of Jerusalem was heard from afar.” What would it mean for the joy of a community of faith to be noticed by those outside it?
